newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour heartened by Clinton re-election.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour heartened by Clinton re-election.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major congratulated U.S. President Bill Clinton on Wednesday on his re-election while the opposition Labour Party said his victory boded well for its own chances in Britain's coming election.
"The prime minister warmly congratulates the president on his re-election. He has won a resounding vote of confidence from the American people," Major's office said in a statement.

"The president has campaigned on his record, and his economic and political achievements have spoken for themselves. The prime minister looks forward to continuing to work closely with the president over the next four years," Major added.
Labour leader Tony Blair, who hopes to oust Major's Conservatives at a general election that must be held by May 22, said he was "absolutely delighted" for Clinton.

"This is a great victory and a personal triumph for the president," Blair said. "He has shown the way that the tide of ideas is turning against the extremes of the right and in favour of progressive politics."

Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown saw the victory as a triumph for progressive politics over conservatism and reaction. "The biggest lesson for Britain is that a campaign that is more about style than substance is a turn-off for voters," he said.

Ministers said Clinton had benefited from the strength of the U.S. economy and were optimistic that Britain's brisk recovery would still bail out the incumbent Conservatives, who trail Labour in polls by about 20 percentage points.
Blair's lieutenants drew different lessons from Clinton's triumph.
Peter Mandelson, Labour's chief election strategist, said the victory showed that a left-of-centre party was "unstoppable" when it fully embraced the centre ground of politics.

"New Labour is building a similar coalition of support based on policies that appeal to the centre and centre-left of British politics. This approach, judging by Mr Clinton's re-election, has proven success," Mandelson said.

Chris Smith, Labour's health spokesman, said Clinton had shown that it was possible to win and win again by sticking to centre-left policies. "I think that is very good news for Tony Blair and the Labour Party," he said.
But Boris Johnson, writing in the Daily Telegraph, said the United States was so different from Britain that both main parties were talking rubbish.

"No analogies with last night's election offer any useful guide to what will happen here next year... To read across from one to the other is like trying to predict the reproductive behaviour of newts by studying the sex-life of dogs," he wrote.
